html:
The Erechtheion is an Ionic temple on the north side of the Acropolis of Athens, built from about 421 to 406 BCE. It is famous for its porch held up by six statues of young women, the Caryatids.

It was the holiest building on the Acropolis, more so than the Parthenon. It housed an ancient olive wood statue of Athena Polias, guardian of the city, which received a new robe at the Panathenaic festival. It also held places linked to the city's myths: the marks of Poseidon's trident, the olive tree that Athena gave Athens, and the tombs of early kings such as Erechtheus. Because the ground is uneven and the shrines were many, the building has an odd shape, with porches on three sides at different levels.

Work began during the Peace of Nicias and went on through the war. Later it became a church, a palace and a harem. Lord Elgin took one of the Caryatids to Britain in the early 19th century, with the Elgin Marbles; the others are now in the Acropolis Museum, replaced on the temple by copies.
